title: Localization of standard cotangent differential augmentations
statement: Let $A\to B$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, $T\subseteq B$ a multiplicative subset, and $C=T^{-1}B$, with its induced $A$-algebra structure. Use the standard complexes $L_{B/A}$ and $L_{C/A}$ of [def-trf-cotangent-resolution-data] in the derived categories of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], and universal differentials [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials]. For $R=B,C$, let $a_R:L_{R/A}\to\Omega^1_{R/A}[0]$ be the differential augmentation: on degree-zero standard-resolution generators it sends $\mathrm dq\otimes r$ to $r\,\mathrm d(\epsilon(q))$, and all other components vanish. For every $B$-module $N$, the canonical tensor/localization identification $N\otimes_B C\cong T^{-1}N$ is given by the mutually inverse maps $n\otimes(b/t)\mapsto bn/t$ and $n/t\mapsto n\otimes(1/t)$. These identifications commute with module maps, and for every cochain complex $K$ of $B$-modules they give $H^i(K\otimes_B C)\cong T^{-1}H^i(K)$ for all integers $i$, naturally in chain maps; in particular degreewise tensor with $C$ preserves quasi-isomorphisms. Let $\lambda:L_{B/A}\otimes_B C\to L_{C/A}$ be the canonical cotangent localization map induced by $B\to C$ and the identity of $A$, and let $\kappa:T^{-1}\Omega^1_{B/A}\to\Omega^1_{C/A}$ send $\mathrm db/t$ to $t^{-1}\mathrm d(b/1)$. Then $\lambda$ is a quasi-isomorphism, $\kappa$ is an isomorphism, and in $D(C)$ one has $a_C\lambda=\kappa[0](a_B\otimes_B C)$, using the displayed tensor/localization identification. On every degree-zero generator $\mathrm dq\otimes(b/t)$ of the localized standard differential complex, both composites in this equality have value $(b/t)\,\mathrm d(\epsilon(q)/1)$. Consequently, if $a_B$ is a quasi-isomorphism, then the canonical map $\kappa^{-1}[0]a_C:L_{C/A}\to(T^{-1}\Omega^1_{B/A})[0]$ is a quasi-isomorphism as well. No nonzero-ring, finite-generation or principal-localization hypothesis is imposed.

proof.text: Define $f_N:N\otimes_B C\to T^{-1}N$ by $f_N(n\otimes b/t)=bn/t$, using tensor bilinearity and the fraction relation in the two cited definitions. Define $g_N(n/t)=n\otimes1/t$. This is independent of fractions: if $u(t'n-tn')=0$, then $n\otimes1/t-n'\otimes1/t'=(t'n-tn')\otimes1/(tt')=u(t'n-tn')\otimes1/(utt')=0$. The same common-denominator formula proves additivity, and moving scalars between tensor factors proves $C$-linearity. Now $f_Ng_N(n/t)=n/t$, while $g_Nf_N(n\otimes b/t)=bn\otimes1/t=n\otimes b/t$. Thus they are inverse. For a $B$-linear $v:N\to N'$, both routes on $n\otimes b/t$ give $bv(n)/t$, proving naturality. Applied degreewise, these maps commute with every differential and chain map.

source.place: Tag 00DK (lemma-tensor-localization), explicit mutually inverse maps with the tensor factors interchanged.

proof.text: For a complex $K$, put $Z^i=\ker d^i$, $I^i=\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}$. Apply exact localization to $0\to Z^i\to K^i\to K^{i+1}$, to $K^{i-1}\to I^i\to0$, and to $0\to I^i\to Z^i\to H^i(K)\to0$. The first identifies the localized cycles with $T^{-1}Z^i$, the second identifies the localized boundaries with $T^{-1}I^i$, and the third identifies their quotient with $T^{-1}H^i(K)$. With step 1 this gives $H^i(K\otimes_B C)\cong T^{-1}H^i(K)$. A chain map sends $z/t$ to its image divided by $t$ at each stage, so the isomorphism is natural. If the chain map is a quasi-isomorphism, its localized cohomology map has inverse obtained by localizing its cohomology inverse; hence termwise tensor preserves quasi-isomorphisms.

source.place: Tag 00CS (proposition-localization-exact), applied to cycles, boundaries and their quotient.

proof.text: Let $P^R_\bullet\to R$ be the standard resolution for $R=B,C$. The universal derivation and the augmentation give an $R$-linear map $\Omega^1_{P^R_0/A}\otimes_{P^R_0}R\to\Omega^1_{R/A}$ by $\mathrm dq\otimes r\mapsto r\,\mathrm d\epsilon_R(q)$. The two faces out of $P^R_1$ have equal composites with $\epsilon_R$, so on $\mathrm dx\otimes r$ their difference maps to $r\,\mathrm d(\epsilon_Rd_0x)-r\,\mathrm d(\epsilon_Rd_1x)=0$. Thus this map, with all other components zero, is a chain map $a_R$. In all other degrees the chain-map equation is zero on both sides, since the target is concentrated in degree zero.

The localization-vanishing lemma applied to $B\to C$ gives $L_{C/B}=0$. The retract lemma, applied to $j=r=\mathrm{id}_A$, gives $L_{A/A}=0$ for the identity of $A$. The map $B\to C$ is flat by the localization-flatness lemma. Apply the zero-relative-square lemma to the square with lower map $A\xrightarrow{1}A$ and upper map $B\to C$. Its last clause identifies the canonical derived comparison with the actual standard chain map $\lambda:L_{B/A}\otimes_B C\to L_{C/A}$ and states that this chain map is a quasi-isomorphism. In particular it applies to arbitrary $T$, including $0\in T$, without a tensor-pushout assumption.

source.place: Tags 08R2 (lemma-when-zero), case (3), and 08SF (lemma-localize), using the canonical-map form recorded by the zero-relative-square node.

proof.text: The differential-localization lemma gives precisely the isomorphism $\kappa$ in the statement. Let $h:P^B_\bullet\to P^C_\bullet$ be the standard map. Its augmentation equation is $\epsilon_C h(q)=\epsilon_B(q)/1$, and its differential map sends $\mathrm dq\otimes(b/t)$ to $\mathrm d(h(q))\otimes(b/t)$. Therefore $a_C\lambda$ sends this generator to $(b/t)\,\mathrm d(\epsilon_B(q)/1)$. The other route first sends it to $\mathrm d\epsilon_B(q)\otimes(b/t)$, which step 1 identifies with $b\,\mathrm d\epsilon_B(q)/t$; applying $\kappa$ gives the same value. Universal differentials generate their modules, and pure tensors generate tensor products, so the degree-zero maps agree. In every other degree both maps to $\Omega^1_{C/A}[0]$ vanish. This proves equality of chain maps, hence the asserted equality in $D(C)$.

source.place: Tag 08QL (section-functoriality), standard map on differential generators; algebra.tex Tag 00RT (lemma-differentials-localize), part (2).

proof.text: If $a_B$ is a quasi-isomorphism, step 2 makes $a_B\otimes_B C$ a quasi-isomorphism. Step 5 says $(\kappa^{-1}[0]a_C)\lambda=a_B\otimes_B C$. On each cohomology module, step 4 makes $H^i(\lambda)$ invertible, so $H^i(\kappa^{-1}[0]a_C)=H^i(a_B\otimes_B C)H^i(\lambda)^{-1}$ is invertible. This is the required quasi-isomorphism. If $0\in T$, then $C$ and all its modules are zero and all displayed maps are the unique isomorphisms; no cancellation by a nonzero element was used. For $T=\{1\}$ the same formulas give identity localization, and nothing in the argument assumes finite generation or a single denominator generating $T$.
